newsitem.title: FRANCE: France braces for rail and civil service strikes.
newsitem.headline: France braces for rail and civil service strikes.

text.p: French unions rejected a government pay offer on Tuesday and called a one-day strike on March 6 by millions of civil servants and public employees, just as the country braced for a rail strike on Wednesday.
Seven trade unions announced the strike just hours after an offer of a 2.8 percent pay rise over 1997 and 1998, condemning government failure to compensate for a pay freeze last year.

"The seven union federations call on civil servants to take part massively in a day of national action, strike and protest rallies on March 6," Bernard Lhubert, head of the civil service branch of the Communist-led CGT union, told reporters.
"They call on the government to open genuine talks on their demands," Lhubert said, reading from a joint union communique.

The swift response came hours before a one-day rail strike called by the CGT from 2300 GMT and a demonstration later on Wednesday by the Socialist CFDT union over rail reforms which both unions see as a threat to jobs and the rail monopoly.

The SNCF state railways said the strike, due to run until 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Thursday, could cut services by up to a half on some main and regional lines. Eurostar high-speed trains from Paris to London and Brussels should be unaffected.

It precedes a strike on Thursday called by unions fighting for a shorter working week and earlier retirement at tram and urban transit companies in towns outside Paris after a similar and effective strike by a wider number of unions last week.

The civil service unions, including moderate ones as well as the militant CGT -- threw down the gauntlet to the centre-right government after an offer from Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben which they had been largely predicting since last week.

Perben told reporters that a "catch-up" for 1996 would have cost 20 billion francs and that the government was determined to show the financial markets and its European Union partners that France would stick firmly to spending restraint as it prepares the economy for a single euro currency.
The CGT dismissed Perben's offer as "pure provocation" and, along with the militant FSU, spoke of extending the protest.
"If the government refuses to budge, we will meet and extend the action," Lhubert of the CGT said. Michel Deschamps of the FSU union added: "there will be a follow-up, that's clear".
The 1996 civil service pay freeze was one of several union gripes behind crippling public sector strikes in late 1995.
Civil servants staged a one-day strike last October 17 over pay and plans to cut their number by nearly 6,000 this year.
About a third of civil servants stayed away from work that day and unions held off follow-up action after Prime Minister Alain Juppe signalled that pay talks could be reopened.
Perben said he was offering the first percent of the 2.8 percent rise in two stages in 1997 and that this, along with automatic increments, would cost about 14 billion francs.
The Wednesday rail strike is expected to cause more limited disruption than a 36-hour stoppage last week, with the CGT going it alone this time round.

It is campaigning, along with the CFDT, against a government plan to set up a state holding company which would take over the bulk of the SNCF's debts of 208 billion francs but which would become owner of the network and charge the SNCF rail usage fees.

Both unions say this amounts to a break-up of the SNCF which could pave the way to allow competitors to move in and also put pressure on jobs and work conditions at a time of cost-cutting, claims denied strongly by Transport Minister Bernard Pons.
